title: VI. Precocity
paragraphs: “What do you think the doctor will tell him?” Kolya asked quickly. “What a repulsive mug he has, though, doesn't he? I can't stand medicine!”
“Ilusha is dying. I think that's certain,” Alyosha answered mournfully.
“They're crooks! Medicine is a fraud! Still, I'm glad to have made your acquaintance, Karamazov. I've wanted to know you for a long time. I'm only sorry we're meeting in such sad circumstances.”
Kolya had a great urge to say something even warmer and more demonstrative, but he felt ill at ease. Alyosha noticed it, smiled, and squeezed his hand.

“I've long learned to respect you as a rare person,” Kolya muttered again, faltering and uncertain. “I've heard you're a mystic, and have been in the monastery. I know you're a mystic, but ... that hasn't put me off. Contact with real life will cure you. It's always that way with characters like yours.”
“What do you mean by mystic? Cure me of what?” Alyosha was rather astonished.
“Oh, God and all the rest of it.”
“What — you don't believe in God?”

“Oh, I've nothing against God. Of course, God is only a hypothesis, but ... I admit He's necessary ... for the order of the universe and so on ... and that if there were no God He would have to be invented,” Kolya added, beginning to blush. He suddenly imagined that Alyosha might think he was showing off his knowledge and trying to prove he was “grown up.” “I haven't the slightest desire to show off my knowledge to him,” Kolya thought indignantly. And all at once he felt horribly annoyed.

“I must admit I can't stand getting into such discussions,” he said with a final air. “It's possible for someone who doesn't believe in God to love humanity, don't you think? Voltaire didn't believe in God, and he loved humanity, didn't he?” (“I'm at it again,” he thought to himself.)

“Voltaire believed in God, though not very much, I think, and I don't think he loved humanity very much either,” Alyosha said quietly, gently, and quite naturally, as though he were talking to someone his own age, or even older. Kolya was particularly struck by Alyosha's apparent diffidence about his opinion of Voltaire. He seemed to be leaving the question open, for him — little Kolya — to settle.
“Have you read Voltaire?” Alyosha finished.
“No, not really ... But I've read _Candide_ in Russian translation ... in an absurd, grotesque old translation. (At it again! Again!)”
“And did you understand it?”

“Oh, yes, all of it. That is ... why do you suppose I wouldn't understand it? There's a lot of nastiness in it, of course. Of course I can understand that it's a philosophical novel, written to advance an idea.” Kolya was getting tangled up by now. “I am a Socialist, Karamazov — I'm an incurable Socialist,” he announced suddenly, out of nowhere.
“A Socialist?” Alyosha laughed. “But when have you had time to become one? Why, I thought you were only thirteen?”
Kolya winced.

“First of all, I am not thirteen, but fourteen — fourteen in a fortnight,” he flushed angrily, “and secondly, I am at a complete loss to understand what my age has to do with it. The question is, what are my convictions — not what is my age, isn't it?”

“When you're older, you'll understand for yourself the influence of age on one's convictions. I also had the impression you weren't expressing your own ideas,” Alyosha answered serenely and modestly, but Kolya cut him off hotly:

“Come, you want obedience and mysticism. You must admit, for instance, that the Christian religion has only been of use to the rich and the powerful to keep the lower classes in slavery. That's so, isn't it?”
“Ah, I know where you read that, and I'm sure someone told you so!” Alyosha cried.

“Come now, what makes you think I read it? And certainly no one told me so. I can think for myself. I'm not opposed to Christ, if you like. He was a most humane person, and if He were alive today, He'd be in the ranks of the revolutionists, and might well play a prominent part. There's no doubt about that.”
“Oh, where, where did you get this from? What fool have you made friends with?” Alyosha exclaimed.
“Come, the truth will out! It just so happens that I've often talked to Mr. Rakitin, of course, but ... old Byelinsky said that too, so they say.”
“Byelinsky? I don't remember. He hasn't written that anywhere.”
“If he didn't write it, they say he said it. I heard it from a ... never mind.”
“And have you read Byelinsky?”
“Well, no ... I haven't read all of him, but ... I read the passage about Tatyana, about why she didn't run off with Onyegin.”
“Didn't run off with Onyegin? Surely you don't ... understand that already?”

“Why, you seem to take me for little Smurov,” Kolya said, with an irritated grin. “But please don't imagine I'm such a revolutionist. I often disagree with Mr. Rakitin. Even though I bring up Tatyana, I'm not at all for the emancipation of women. I admit that women are a subject race and must obey. _Les femmes tricottent_, as Napoleon said.” Kolya smiled for some reason. “On that question at least, I'm quite in agreement with that pseudo-great man. I also think that leaving one's own country and fleeing to America is mean — worse than mean, silly. Why go to America when one can be of great service to humanity right here? Now, especially. There's a huge amount of fruitful work open to us. That's what I answered.”
“What do you mean? Answered whom? Has someone already suggested you go to America?”

“I must admit, they've been at me to go, but I refused. That's between ourselves, of course, Karamazov — do you hear, not a word to anyone. I'm telling you this only. I'm not at all eager to fall into the clutches of the secret police and take lessons at the Chain bridge.
Long will you remember The house at the Chain bridge.

Do you remember? It's splendid. Why are you laughing? You don't suppose I'm lying, do you?” (“What if he finds out I've only got the one number of _The Bell_ in father's bookcase, and haven't read any more of it?” Kolya thought with a shudder.)

“Oh no, I'm not laughing, and I don't suppose for a moment that you're lying. No, indeed, I can't think that — because all this, alas, is perfectly true. But tell me, have you read Pushkin — _Onyegin_, for example?... You were speaking about Tatyana just now.”
“No, I haven't read it yet, but I want to. I have no prejudices, Karamazov; I want to hear both sides. What makes you ask?”
“Oh, nothing.”

“Tell me, Karamazov, do you have an awful contempt for me?” Kolya rapped out suddenly, drawing himself up in front of Alyosha as though on drill. “Be so kind as to tell me without beating around the bush.”
“Contempt for you?” Alyosha looked at him in wonder. “What for? I'm only sad that a charming nature such as yours should be perverted by all this crude nonsense before you've even begun to live.”
“Don't worry about my nature,” Kolya interrupted, not without complacency. “But it's true I'm stupidly sensitive, crudely sensitive. You just smiled, and I imagined you seemed to —”

“Oh, my smile meant something quite different. I'll tell you why I smiled. Not long ago I read the criticism a German who had lived in Russia made about our students and schoolboys of today. ‘Show a Russian schoolboy,' he writes, ‘a map of the stars, which he knows nothing about, and he'll bring you back the map the next day with corrections on it.' No knowledge and unbounded conceit — that's what the German was saying about the Russian schoolboy.”

“Yes, that's absolutely right,” Kolya suddenly laughed. “Exactly so! Bravo, German! But he didn't see the good side — what do you think? Conceit, yes — that comes from youth, and it will be corrected if need be; but on the other hand, there's an independent spirit almost from childhood, boldness of thought and conviction, not the spirit of these sausage makers, groveling before authority. Still, the German was right all the same. Bravo, German! But the Germans should be strangled all the same. Though they're so good at science and learning, they must be strangled.”
“Strangled, what for?” Alyosha smiled.

“Well, perhaps I'm talking nonsense, I admit. I'm awfully childish sometimes, and when I'm pleased about anything I can't restrain myself and am ready to talk all kinds of rubbish. But look here, we're chattering away here about nothing, and that doctor's been in there a long time. But perhaps he's examining mamma and that poor crippled Nina. I liked that Nina, you know. As I was leaving she whispered to me suddenly, ‘Why didn't you come before?' And in such a voice, so reproachfully! I think she's awfully nice and touching.”

“Yes, yes! Well, you'll be coming often; you'll see what she's like. It would do you a great deal of good to know people like her — to learn to value a great deal that you'll only find out by knowing these people,” Alyosha observed warmly. “That would have more effect on you than anything.”
“Oh, how I regret and blame myself for not having come sooner!” Kolya exclaimed, with bitter feeling.
“Yes, it's a great pity. You saw for yourself how delighted the poor child was to see you. And how he fretted for you to come!”

“Don't tell me! You're making it worse! But it serves me right. What kept me from coming was my conceit, my egoistic vanity, and the beastly willfulness I can never seem to shake, though I've struggled with it all my life. I see that now. I am a beast in many ways, Karamazov!”
“No, you have a charming nature, though it's been distorted, and I quite understand why you have had such an influence on this generous, morbidly sensitive boy,” Alyosha answered warmly.
“And you say that to me!” Kolya cried. “And would you believe it, I thought — I've thought several times since I've been here — that you despised me! If you only knew how I prize your opinion!”
“But are you really so sensitive? At your age! Would you believe it, just now, as you were telling your story, I thought, watching you, that you must be very sensitive!”

“You thought so? What an eye you have, I say! I bet that was when I was talking about the goose. That was exactly when I was imagining you had a great contempt for me for being in such a hurry to show off, and for a moment I actually hated you for it, and began talking like a fool. Then I imagined — just now, here — when I said that if there were no God He would have to be invented, that I was in too great a hurry to parade my knowledge, especially since I got that phrase out of a book. But I swear I wasn't showing off out of vanity, though I really don't know why. Because I was so pleased? Yes, I think it was because I was so pleased ... though it's perfectly disgraceful for anyone to start gushing the moment he's pleased, I know that. But I'm convinced now that you don't despise me — it was all in my imagination. Oh, Karamazov, I'm profoundly unhappy. I sometimes imagine all sorts of things — that everyone is laughing at me, the whole world, and then I feel ready to overturn the whole order of things.”
“And you worry everyone around you,” Alyosha smiled.
“Yes, I worry everyone around me, especially my mother. Karamazov, tell me — am I very ridiculous now?”

“Don't think about that, don't think about it at all!” Alyosha cried. “And what does ridiculous mean? Isn't everyone constantly being or seeming ridiculous? Besides, nearly all clever people now are terribly afraid of being ridiculous, and that makes them unhappy. The only thing that surprises me is that you should be feeling it so early, though I've noticed it for some time, and not only in you. Nowadays even the children have begun to suffer from it. It's almost a kind of insanity. The devil has taken the form of that vanity and entered into the whole generation; it's simply the devil,” Alyosha added, without a trace of the smile Kolya, staring at him, had expected to see. “You are like everyone else,” Alyosha said in conclusion, “that is, like a great many others. Only you must not be like everyone else — that's all.”
“Even if everyone is like that?”

“Yes, even if everyone is like that. Be the one who is not. You really are not like everyone else — here you're not ashamed to confess to something bad, and even ridiculous. And who will admit that much these days? No one. People have even stopped feeling the impulse to self-criticism. Don't be like everyone else, even if you're the only one.”

“Splendid! I wasn't mistaken in you. You know how to console a person. Oh, how I've longed to know you, Karamazov! I've long been eager for this meeting. Can you really have thought about me, too? You said just now that you had thought of me?”
“Yes, I'd heard about you and thought about you, too ... and if it's partly vanity that makes you ask — well, it doesn't matter.”
“You know, Karamazov, our talk has been like a declaration of love,” said Kolya, in a bashful, melting voice. “That's not ridiculous, is it?”
“Not at all ridiculous, and even if it were, it wouldn't matter, because it's been a good thing.” Alyosha smiled brightly.
“But you know, Karamazov, you must admit that you're a little ashamed yourself, right now ... I can see it in your eyes.” Kolya smiled with a kind of sly happiness.
“Why ashamed?”
“Well, why are you blushing?”
“It was you who made me blush,” Alyosha laughed, and he really did blush. “Oh, well, I am a little, goodness knows why — I don't know...” he muttered, almost embarrassed.

“Oh, how I love you and admire you at this moment, precisely because you're a little ashamed yourself! Because you are just like me!” Kolya cried, in positive ecstasy. His cheeks glowed, his eyes beamed.
“You know, Kolya, you're going to be very unhappy in life,” something made Alyosha say suddenly.
“I know, I know. How you know it all in advance!” Kolya agreed at once.
“But you'll bless life on the whole, all the same.”

“Exactly — hurrah! You're a prophet. Oh, we'll get on together, Karamazov! Do you know what delights me most? That you treat me entirely like an equal. But we are not equals, no, we are not — you are better. But we'll get on. Do you know, all this last month I've been saying to myself, ‘Either we'll be friends at once, forever, or we'll part as enemies to the grave!'”
“And saying that, of course, you loved me,” Alyosha laughed gaily.
“I did. I loved you awfully. I've been loving you and dreaming of you. And how is it you know everything in advance? Ah, here's the doctor. Goodness! What will he tell us? Look at his face!”
